text.p: Unexploited high-quality diamond fields in Sierra Leone will help secure a brilliant future for Toronto-quoted Rex Diamond Mining Corp, the company's chief executive said on Tuesday.
"We have by what is known today about $4.9 billion worth of reserves of gem-quality diamonds," Rex's Belgian CEO and chairman Serge Muller told Reuters in an interview.

Rex announced last month the value of the Tongo field, one of the fields in Sierra Leone on which it owns leases, was estimated by a leading expert at $3.3 billion with resources totalling 18.9 million carats.
Rex also operates three fissure diamond mines in South Africa and sorting and marketing facilities in the Belgian port of Antwerp, the world's leading rough diamond trading centre.

Muller said annual output at Rex's fields in South Africa and Sierra Leone could amount to 600,000 carats in five years, two thirds of it coming from Sierra Leone, giving it total revenue of $120 million a year at an average of $200 a carat.

"This would give us gross profit of around $50 million a year," he said. The company had a $1.7 million 1996 net profit and $2.5 million 1996 gross profit and produced 51,851 carats of rough diamonds with an average value of $248 per carat.
The start-up of Tongo fields is expected to take about two to three years. Production at the Zimmi diamond mining area is expected to start mid-1998, he said.
Muller, 40, said Rex was considering a capital increase at a later stage to help finance growth, bringing the total number of shares to about 50 million.
Rex, which was listed in Toronto last year, now has 34.6 million shares with more than half owned by management.

Large institutions -- mainly Canadian mutual funds, British life insurance firms and large Swiss banks -- have Rex stock in portfolio with about two million shares believed to be held by private investors, he said.
"Obviously when you want to open up large mines like Tongo fields...a capital increase will be necessary, but it's not immediate," said Muller, adding he might list Rex elsewhere.
"I've been looking at (European small cap market) Easdaq and watching carefully to see how it is evolving. A possibility is there, we're not a pure Canadian company," he said.
But he had no plans to diversify," he added.

Muller, who has been working under four different administrations in Sierra Leone in the past 12 years, said there was no threat to investors following December's peace deal between the government and rebels, who took up arms in 1991.

He noted that Rex might employ 2,000 to 3,000 people in Sierra Leone, which would make it the country's second largest employer after the government. "As long as you don't meddle in politics, you don't have problems," he said.
He expected other mining companies to be lured to Sierra Leone but played down competition. "The mines we have there are the most important parts that can be had," he said.
Muller also said he was busy exploring a potentially major field in another country but declined to give further details.
He said Rex also stood out because of its focus on gem-quality stones, which represent just 18 percent of total world diamond production but 62 percent of total value.
With three quarters of production over one carat, Rex is bound to profit from the expected price increase for gem-quality rough stones.
"In gems, you have very little supply compared to demand so prices should strengthen, in large stones even more," he said.
"If you know that the world average is $57 a carat, you can appreciate what it means being in gem diamonds. I can sell our production many times a day, I have more buyers than production," he said.
Muller also noted he was not selling his gems through the De Beers Central Selling Organisation.
"I sell straight to cutters, I sell everything in Antwerp," he said.
He said that North America, which traditionally bought cheaper diamonds, was now emerging as a buyer of better quality diamonds, taking the place of Japan.
But the revival of the Japanese market should further bolster the high-end diamond market.
"When the Japanese economy gets out of its down cycle again it will have to compete with the American consumer for the better stones," he said.
